The Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS) provides comprehensive health and safety information on the safe use of hazardous products in Canadian workplaces.
The main components of WHMIS are hazard identification and product classification, labelling, safety data sheets, and worker education and training.
Canada has aligned the Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS) with the Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS).

Aligning WHMIS with GHS provides more comprehensive hazard classification criteria that better indicate hazard severity, includes new hazard classes, makes physical hazard criteria consistent with the Transport of Dangerous Goods (TDG) regulations, and standardizes hazard and precautionary statements and the safety data sheet format with more comprehensive requirements.

A generic chemical identity listed on a safety data sheet indicates that the supplier has applied to have the exact ingredients in the hazardous product considered as confidential business information (CBI).
Having an ingredient considered as confidential business information requires following a strict process, and approval is granted only by Health Canada.

Consumer products are labelled according to other legislation, and a comprehensive chemical safety program would include both WHMIS-regulated hazardous products and any other products workers may be exposed to, including consumer products, for which workers should still receive education and training on safe use.

All hazardous products used in the workplace are covered by the WHMIS regulations, and employers are required under WHMIS to educate and train workers on the hazards and safe use of these products as part of a WHMIS program.

WHMIS does not cover explosives as defined in the Explosives Act; cosmetics, devices, drugs, or food as defined in the Food and Drugs Act; pest control products as defined in the Pest Control Products Act; consumer products as defined in the Canada Consumer Product Safety Act; wood or products made of wood; radioactive nuclear substances within the meaning of the Nuclear Safety and Control Act; hazardous waste, meaning a hazardous product sold for recycling or recovery or intended for disposal; tobacco and tobacco products as defined in the Tobacco and Vaping Products Act; and manufactured articles.
Products exempt from WHMIS label and safety data sheet requirements may still have hazards, and employers must still provide education and training on their health effects, safe use, and storage.
Consumer products are products that can be purchased in a store and are generally intended for use in the home, often including cleaning products, adhesives, or lubricants.
Under WHMIS, a product covered by the Hazardous Products Act that meets the criteria to be included in a hazard class or category is considered to be a hazardous product.

Suppliers must compare their products against the specific hazard classification criteria set out in the Hazardous Products Regulations to determine whether a product is a WHMIS-regulated hazardous product.
Workers must read, understand, and follow the instructions on the label and safety data sheet, and match the product name in Section 1 of the safety data sheet to the label.
Under WHMIS, each hazard class or category must use the specified pictograms and other label elements to indicate the hazard that is present and the precautionary measures that must be taken.

Section 2 of a safety data sheet covers the product's potential hazards but may not specify the safe work procedures needed for a particular workplace, for example stating only that a respirator is needed without specifying the type.
Workers should ask for a new label when a product's old label is not visible or readable, and should not use a product that is not labelled or whose label is unreadable.
Employers and workers use the information provided by the WHMIS label and safety data sheet to be informed and to know how to safely use, handle, store, and dispose of hazardous products.

Workers should know a hazardous product's hazards, precautions, and emergency actions from Section 2 of its safety data sheet, its safe handling and storage instructions from Section 7, and what to do in an emergency from Sections 4, 5 and 6.
WHMIS is enforced by the provincial or territorial government departments or agencies responsible for health and safety, or by the Labour Program for federally regulated workplaces.

WHMIS is also regulated in the workplace by the provinces, territories and federal (for federally regulated workplaces) governments under their occupational health and safety legislation, and while these jurisdictions based their WHMIS regulations on a common model, small variations between jurisdictions may exist.
WHMIS supplier requirements are regulated by the federal legislation consisting of the Hazardous Products Act (HPA) and the Hazardous Products Regulations (HPR).
The federal, provincial, and territorial occupational health and safety WHMIS regulations may also require updating.
WHMIS first became law in 1988 through a series of complementary federal, provincial and territorial legislation and regulations, and this original system is identified as WHMIS 1988.
WHMIS requirements are implemented through coordinated and interlocking Health Canada and federal, provincial and territorial occupational health and safety laws.

Updates to the Hazardous Products Act and Hazardous Products Regulations came into force on December 15, 2022, and suppliers have a 3-year transition period until December 15, 2025 to bring product classifications, safety data sheets and labels into compliance with the amendments.
Health Canada is the government body responsible for the overall WHMIS supplier-related laws.

Employers must provide workers access to up-to-date safety data sheets, ensure hazardous products are properly labelled, prepare workplace labels as needed, prepare safety data sheets when necessary such as when they manufacture a hazardous product used on-site, and ensure appropriate control measures are in place to protect worker health and safety.
Suppliers and employers must use and follow the WHMIS requirements for labels and safety data sheets (SDSs) for hazardous products sold, distributed, or imported into Canada.

An importer of hazardous products may keep the foreign supplier's name, address and telephone number on the safety data sheet obtained from that supplier and on the label, as provided under Part 5 – Exemptions of the Hazardous Products Regulations.
Under WHMIS, an employer who imports a hazardous product only for use in their own workplace is considered to be the importer and is responsible for compliance with all WHMIS supplier requirements.

Under WHMIS, a supplier is a person who, in the course of business, sells or imports a hazardous product; a manufacturer is a supplier who, in the course of business in Canada, manufactures, produces, processes, packages or labels a hazardous product and sells it; an importer is a supplier who brings a hazardous product into Canada but does not sell the product; and a distributor is a Canadian supplier to whom a hazardous product was sold and who then resells it without modifying it in any way.

All hazardous products must be labelled according to the Hazardous Products Regulations and must have a corresponding safety data sheet provided to the purchaser at the time of sale, with the hazard class and category provided in Section 2 (Hazard Identification) of the safety data sheet and on the supplier label.

Under WHMIS, suppliers and importers are responsible for meeting the requirements of the Hazardous Products Act and regulations, including determining the appropriate classification of hazardous products, providing labels, and providing safety data sheets.

Employers who produce hazardous products within their workplace for use in that workplace must follow WHMIS supplier requirements: assess and classify the product's hazards, create and apply a workplace label to the product or its container, and prepare a safety data sheet meeting the Hazardous Products Act supplier requirements.
Under WHMIS, an importer is a supplier who brings a hazardous product into Canada but does not sell the product.

In regulated manufacturing environments, quality inspection generates the objective evidence—measurements, test results, and documentation—that proves conformance, and Quality Control feeds that evidence into corrective action systems, process improvements, and supplier feedback loops.
Production-stage quality inspection covers four phases: Incoming (IQC), In-Process (IPQC), Final (FQC), and Outgoing (OQC).

Quality inspection is a point-in-time verification that a product meets specifications, while Quality Control (QC) is the broader feedback system that uses inspection data to drive correction and improvement.
In practice, quality inspection is the systematic process of measuring, testing, and documenting whether a product meets its design specifications before it moves forward in the supply chain.
Inspected products can be the components used for production, semi-finished goods, or, most often, finished goods before shipment to a customer.
Quality inspections in precision manufacturing cover five core areas, including physical dimensions and geometric tolerances, material conformity, and performance and functionality.

Quality inspection is defined in the ISO 2859 standard, which is derived from MIL-STD 105 E, as an activity such as measuring, examining, testing or gauging one or more characteristics of a product and comparing the results with specified requirements in order to establish whether conformity is achieved for each characteristic.
Quality inspections typically take place before, during, and after production.

Quality inspection comprises the stages Incoming Quality Control (IQC), In-Process Quality Control (IPQC), and Final/PSI, each addressing a distinct point in the production lifecycle and applying broadly across industries, plus specialized inspection types used in precision manufacturing that operate within those stages for aerospace, defense, and high-tolerance work.
In quality control, the term inspection refers to the activity of checking products, whereas audit applies to analyzing manufacturing processes and/or systems.

The American Society for Quality (ASQ) defines quality inspection as a verification activity in which one or more product characteristics are examined and compared against specified requirements to assess conformity.
Every effective quality inspection follows five steps: define criteria, sample, inspect, document, then correct.
Checking quality only at the end of production is very risky.

Final inspection, also called pre-shipment inspection (FQC/PSI), is the last checkpoint before products move to stock or shipment, with the entire finished product measured against engineering specifications, customer requirements, and applicable standard.

In-process inspection (IPQC) assesses workflow adherence to documented procedures, dimensional accuracy at critical manufacturing stages, tooling calibration and machine setup validation, and worker skill validation and process capability.

In-process inspections occur while production is underway, typically when 10–15% of units are complete, with the goal of catching deviations early before they become systemic failures affecting entire production runs.

The "1-10-100 rule" demonstrates that defects costing $1 to fix during production cost $10 at final inspection and $100 (or more) post-delivery, so catching defects mid-production prevents compounding waste and rework costs.

Incoming Quality Control is critical for new suppliers without proven quality history, large contracts where defects would create significant financial exposure, high-risk materials such as aerospace alloys and safety-critical components, and materials with long lead times where rework would delay production.

For proven suppliers with consistent quality records, ISO 2859-3 skip-lot sampling reduces inspection costs by randomly accepting lots without full inspection, with acceptance based on specified probabilities rather than 100% review.

Incoming Quality Control (IQC) is the quality inspection stage that occurs before raw materials or components enter the production line, in which inspectors verify that incoming materials conform to purchase order specifications, check for shipping damage, and validate supplier documentation including material certificates and test reports.
A factory usually cannot turn defective inputs, such as components or raw materials, into good products, and problems are much harder to detect once the materials are embedded in the final product.

To decrease quality risks, inputs can be inspected prior to production, with random samples checked visually or sent to a laboratory for tests, and the buyer should clearly define what inputs are acceptable before giving any order.
Strong quality inspection programs combine trained inspectors, standardized checklists, and real-time data to drive continuous improvement.

The quality inspector usually follows a pre-established checklist based on the product specifications, using it to guide the control process and check whether production conforms to the specifications.
Each test in a quality inspection may require specific training and equipment, for example testing a watch's accuracy.
Products are checked either by the buyer's own inspectors or by an external agency appointed by the buyer, known as first party QC, or by the supplier's quality controllers, known as second party QC.
There is no such thing as 'third party quality control', even though this is a common phrase.
The choice of quality inspection solution depends on the risks in production.
Hundreds of thousands of first-party inspectors travel to factories daily in China, Vietnam, India, and other low-cost Asian countries.
Buyers have mainly three tools at their disposal to check the quality of their suppliers' products, and each buyer should try to choose the solutions that best fit their needs.
When buying from China, Vietnam, India, or another low-cost country, quality inspections should be performed by third-party QC providers appointed by the buyer or by the buyer's own inspectors.
Specialized quality inspection types include First Article Inspection (FAI), source inspection, and returned material inspection.

Quality inspection types are categorized two ways: by production stage, which is most common in manufacturing quality control, and by purpose, which is used in supply chain and regulated industries, and both frameworks overlap and complement each other.

During a pre-production inspection, an experienced inspector can examine the making of a prototype or sample to verify that the factory understood the technical files and knows what product the client wants.
Sometimes production has already started when a pre-production inspection takes place.

Examining the making of a prototype or sample during a pre-production inspection also verifies that the development team clearly communicated the requirements to the manufacturing team and that the equipment for mass production is similar to that used for making prototypes.
Pre-production inspection, also known as "initial production inspection", is one of the three most common types of quality inspections.
Photos and/or videos should be captured all along the way during a quality inspection, and Microsoft Word makes it easy to prepare places for photos.

In the conformity to specifications section of an inspection report, the inspector uses the product specifications as a checklist, with typical points covering materials, workmanship, appearance, labeling, inner packing, and outer packing.
The conformity to specifications section of an inspection report also includes measurements.
The conformity to specifications section of an inspection report also includes special tests, for example tests for safety and function.

In 13 years of providing quality inspection services, the provider recalls only a few large companies pushing to use the client's own template, while all SMEs were fine with the provider using its own template.
Most companies have defined an inspection report template, which typically includes a conformity to specifications section.
A quality assurance agency will have its own inspection report template by default, so make sure to see a sample report before working with one.
Most quality inspection types use ISO 2859-1 Acceptance Quality Limit (AQL) sampling methodology to balance risk and efficiency.

For proven suppliers with consistent quality records, ISO 2859-3 skip-lot sampling reduces inspection costs by randomly accepting lots without full inspection, with acceptance based on specified probabilities rather than 100% review.

In a quality inspection, the inspector picks samples and asks whether a consumer or user would accept the product if it is sold to users, or whether the part would create issues down the road if it is to be further processed or assembled.
